newsitem.title: USA: US bank panel votes to approve bank/commerce mix.
newsitem.headline: US bank panel votes to approve bank/commerce mix.

text.p: The House Banking Committee voted on Tuesday in favor of allowing banks to engage in a limited amount of commercial activity.
The committee is debating a bill to comprehensively overhaul U.S. banking laws and allow banks to freely enter other financial sectors like insurance and securities underwriting.
The committee voted 35-19 to adopt an amendment that would allow a company that owned a bank to derive up to 15 percent of its gross revenues from a "basket" of commercial activity.

Under the amendment, banks would not be able to engage directly in commercial activity and bank holding companies could not affiliate with commercial companies that had more than $750 million of assets.
After the vote, the committee adjourned until 1000 EDT (1400 GMT) on Wednesday.
"We have to have a commerce component here," Rep Marge Roukema, one of the amendment's sponsors, argued. "I believe it's the reality of our time."

The New Jersey Republican had previously supported a broader basket with a 25 percent revenue test, but that drew opposition from committee chairman Jim Leach and Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, along with small banks and consumer groups and others. Senate Democrats are also largely opposed to mixing commerce and banking.

The Clinton administration had been leaning in favor of allowing banking and commerce earlier this year, but last month in its bank reform proposal it did not take a definitive position. Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato has sponsored legislation in the Senate allowing mixing.
The compromise amendment was adopted easily but won over few of the opponents of earlier, broader proposals.

"The amendment is so expansive that it's tantamount to suggesting that you don't need control rods in a nuclear power plant," ranking Democrat Henry Gonzalez of Texas said. "This amendment goes beyond anyone's need for accomodation."

"There is no economic rationale that has been presented to the commitee that says this is good for the economy," Leach said at the hearing. "There's no consensus anywhere on the need to tear down these walls."

The amendment was also sponsored by Rep Richard Baker, Republican of Louisiana, who has favored nearly unlimited mixing of banking and commerce, and Democrats John LaFalce of New York and Bruce Vento of Minnesota.

The banking committee is considering 91 amendments to bank reform legislation that would repeal the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act. If the bill is approved by the committee, it next goes to the Commerce Committee before being considered by the full House of Representatives. Rep Bill McCollum, Republican of Florida, said he would introduce an amendment Wednesday known as a "reverse basket" to allow commercial companies to derive a limited amount of their revenues from financial activities.
